- Paper: "ChatGPT's Ontological Landscape" (William L. Benzon) — examines how ChatGPT organizes and traverses categories/concepts when generating lists and answers
  - Student's "give me 20 things" experiment
    - Probes the same phenomenon Benzon studies: how ChatGPT structures a semantic/ontological space when asked to enumerate items
    - Observed pattern (butterfly, dragonfly, ... -> flying bugs -> general bugs -> flying mammals -> general mammals under "50 more") is an empirical trace of the model drifting across nested ontological categories
    - Acts as a small independent replication/extension of Benzon's landscape idea: category boundaries are soft and the model "walks" from a narrow lexical pattern into broader superordinate categories as it runs out of close matches
  - Student's 20 Questions experiment
    - Directly tests the abstract/concrete axis, one of the ontological distinctions Benzon's paper treats as structuring ChatGPT's conceptual space
    - Hypothesis (first question defaults to abstract/concrete because abstract vocabulary is smaller) is a mechanistic guess about *why* the ontological landscape is shaped the way Benzon describes
    - Identified confound (concrete/abstract word distribution in the dictionary vs. in the experiment) shows the student pushing back on their own claim before trusting it
    - Controlled follow-up (equal concrete/abstract word list given to ChatGPT) is a targeted test of whether the bias is a genuine ontological asymmetry (Benzon's territory) or just a sampling artifact
    - Null result (no significant bias once the list is balanced) suggests the asymmetry isn't baked into ChatGPT's ontology itself, but is an artifact of word frequency — a data point that qualifies rather than confirms the paper's framing
